profile.summary: This is the evaluation framework published with MochiBind, a study of whether antibody-antigen affinity predictors generalise to antigens they have never seen. The data are the four antigen systems of the AlphaBind dataset, PP489, PEM, VHH72 and TRA, each a large pool of antibody variants with measured affinities. The task is posed pairwise: given two antibodies against the same antigen, say which binds more strongly. Antigens are rotated so that each in turn is the held-out test antigen while two train and one validates, which means the test antigen is absent from training entirely. Scoring is pairwise accuracy over 200,000 sampled test pairs per antigen, plus retrieval accuracy and precision at K after a global ranking is derived with TrueSkill. Anyone comparing sequence-based and structure-based affinity predictors for candidate ranking can use it as a cross-antigen generalisation test.

summary_quotes.text: we establish a benchmarking framework for evaluating universal antibody-antigen binding affinity prediction. Our framework compares sequence- and structure-based methods across diverse antigens, introducing standardized evaluation protocols based on pairwise accuracy and retrieval metrics.

To rigorously assess the models’ performance on out-of-distribution systems, we employ a cross-antigen evaluation scheme. In each experimental configuration, two antigens are used for training (400,000 pairs), one for validation (200,000 pairs), and one for testing (200,000 pairs without threshold). For example, when the model is trained on PEM and PP489, the VHH72 dataset is used for validation to select the best-performing checkpoint, and the model is subsequently evaluated on TRA. This process is repeated so that each antigen serves as the held-out test set once.
To complement retrieval-based evaluation, we also assessed the pairwise prediction accuracy, which quantifies a model’s ability to correctly identify the stronger binder within sampled pairs.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a predictor can rank antibodies against an antigen it was never trained on. The authors' stated reason for building the framework is that studies in this area differ in dataset curation, splitting and metrics, so models cannot be compared, and that most published models are evaluated in-sample. Two things are measured. Pairwise accuracy asks whether the stronger of two antibodies is identified correctly. Retrieval accuracy and precision at K ask whether the strong binders can be pulled out of a large pool, which is what an in silico screening campaign actually needs. The authors argue that ranking and retrieval are more robust than absolute regression when affinity measurements are noisy.

quotes.text: we establish a benchmarking framework for evaluating universal antibody-antigen binding affinity prediction. Our framework compares sequence- and structure-based methods across diverse antigens, introducing standardized evaluation protocols based on pairwise accuracy and retrieval metrics.

To evaluate the retrieval performance, we propose two metrics in our evaluation framework: retrieval accuracy and retrieval precision. Retrieval accuracy calculates the percentage of antibodies from the K highest-ranked candidates that are among the true top-binding antibodies, while retrieval precision measures the percentage of good binders captured within the model’s recommendations, relative to the total number of good binders possible in this group.
To complement retrieval-based evaluation, we also assessed the pairwise prediction accuracy, which quantifies a model’s ability to correctly identify the stronger binder within sampled pairs.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data come from the AlphaBind dataset, which holds four antigen systems: AAB-PP489, a humanoid scFv against human TIGIT; Pembrolizumab-scFv against PD-1; VHH72, a camelid single-chain antibody against the SARS-CoV-1 RBD with cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2; and Trastuzumab-scFv against human HER2. The paper states that each system contains approximately 30,000 antibody variants generated and validated with AlphaSeq. For this benchmark the pools are cut down by stratified sampling to keep the affinity distribution: 5,000 antibodies are drawn from the fine-tuning set and 5,000 from the evaluation set for PP489, PEM and VHH72, giving 10,000 variants each, while 5,000 are drawn for TRA. The four antigens have almost no sequence similarity to one another: Needleman-Wunsch global alignment with BLOSUM62 gives off-diagonal normalised scores between minus 0.053 and 0.034. Pairs are then sampled, 200,000 per antigen, and the training pairs are restricted to those whose relative affinity difference exceeds 10 per cent while the test pairs carry no such threshold. The published sampling script differs from the paper here: as shipped it samples up to 500,000 pairs per antigen with the threshold set to 0 and writes sampled_pairs_500k_0th.pkl, so the released sampler is not the configuration the paper describes, and the 10 per cent value survives in it only as a function default. The script also adds a condition the paper does not mention: a pair is only eligible if both antibody sequences have the same length.

quotes.text: This dataset contains four unique antigens, each with thousands of experimentally characterized antibody candidates covering a wide affinity range: (1) AAB-PP489 (PP489), a previously undescribed humanoid scFv targeting human TIGIT; (2) Pembrolizumab-scFv (PEM), a humanized mouse antibody formatted as an scFv targeting PD-1; (3) VHH72, a camelid single-chain antibody targeting the RBD of SARS-CoV-1 with cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2; and (4) Trastuzumab-scFv (TRA), a humanized mouse antibody targeting human HER2.
Each antigen system contains approximately 30 000 antibody variants generated and validated using AlphaSeq.

To reduce computational cost while maintaining data diversity, we applied stratified sampling to select 5,000 antibodies per antigen following the same binding-affinity distribution as the full AlphaBind dataset. This sampling strategy follows the experimental design of the original AlphaBind study, in which PP489, PEM, and VHH72 are used for both finetuning and evaluation, while TRA is treated as a held-out antigen system for assessing cross-antigen generalization. As a result, for PP489, PEM, and VHH72, we sample 5,000 variants from the finetuning set and 5,000 from the evaluation set, yielding 10,000 antibody variants per antigen. In contrast, 5,000 variants are sampled from the TRA dataset.

Pairwise antigen similarity was quantified using Needleman-Wunsch global alignment with BLOSUM62 substitution matrix, with the gap-opening penalty set to −10 and the gap-extension penalty set to −0.5. These are standard setups for algorithms (e.g., BLAST) and many protein alignment tools. Scores were normalized by the maximum self-alignment score to account for sequence length differences. The off-diagonal scores among the four antigen systems were all close to zero or negative, ranging from −0.053 to 0.034, indicating very low global sequence similarity between these antigens.

Specifically, we sample 200,000 pairs per antigen for training, restricting selected pairs to those whose relative affinity difference exceeds 10%. This threshold ensures that the selected pairs reflect meaningful distinctions in binding strength, promoting efficient learning of robust and interpretable signals.
For the test datasets, no such thresholding is applied, allowing evaluation under realistic experimental conditions that include small and noisy affinity differences.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is given two antibodies against the same antigen and must say which binds more strongly. The split is a rotation over antigens: in each configuration two antigens supply 400,000 training pairs, one supplies 200,000 validation pairs used to pick the checkpoint, and the fourth supplies 200,000 test pairs with no affinity-difference threshold, and the rotation is repeated so that every antigen is the test antigen once. Pairwise accuracy is the share of test pairs ordered correctly, and Table 2 reports it per held-out antigen for each method. Significance against each baseline is tested with a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs, with all p values below 0.0001. For retrieval, pairwise predictions are turned into a global ranking with the TrueSkill algorithm, then retrieval accuracy and retrieval precision at K are computed; in the precision figure an antibody with log Kd below 2, Kd in nanomolar, counts as a good binder. Complex-wise baselines are handled on their own terms: Boltz-2 and GeoDock supply structure-derived confidence scores used as proxies rather than trained affinity predictions, and Graphinity is reported after fine-tuning on the training split because the published model, trained on single-point mutations, did not perform well on this data.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The code is published as a reproducibility release. The repository holds MochiBind checkpoints for each of the four antigen systems, the sampled AlphaBind CSV files and the preprocessed pair pickles, the model and training code, and notebooks for pairwise accuracy and for the Graphinity, GeoDock and Boltz-2 retrieval comparisons. The README gives a conda environment and a requirements install, an embedding generation step and a training entry point at model_src/main_mean.py, and notes that full training expects precomputed ESM mean embeddings in a data_processed_esm_mean directory. The release terms matter: the repository is CC BY-NC 4.0 and the README states it is a non-commercial research release, published for academic reproducibility, with pull requests not accepted so that the code stays as it was used in the paper. The underlying AlphaBind data are MIT licensed, which the README states and links.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Pairwise accuracy is the headline for the comparison in Table 2: the percentage of test pairs in which the stronger binder is identified correctly, higher is better, with significance against each baseline from a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test. Two retrieval metrics complement it, both higher is better: retrieval accuracy, the share of the K highest-ranked candidates that are among the true top binders, and retrieval precision, the share of good binders captured among the recommendations relative to the good binders available. The authors argue for ranking and retrieval over absolute regression metrics such as mean absolute error or correlation.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three: Graphinity, an equivariant graph neural network on structural inputs, reported after fine-tuning on the training split because the released model, trained on single-point mutations, did not perform well here; and two structure-derived proxy scorers, Boltz-2, used through its ipLDDT score, and GeoDock. MochiBind, the authors' own sequence-only pairwise model built on ESM-2 embeddings, is the method under test.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split itself is the control, and it is the point of the benchmark: the training, validation and test sets cover distinct antigen systems with no overlap, so the test antigen is unseen. Two further things support it. The four antigens have near-zero global sequence similarity to one another, measured by Needleman-Wunsch alignment with BLOSUM62 and normalised, between minus 0.053 and 0.034. And within an antigen the variants come from one seed framework with varied multi-point mutations, which the authors say forces models to learn binding determinants rather than memorising identities. Nothing is said about overlap between the AlphaBind antibodies and the training data of the pretrained ESM-2 model or of the structure-based baselines.

quotes.text: Pairwise antigen similarity was quantified using Needleman-Wunsch global alignment with BLOSUM62 substitution matrix, with the gap-opening penalty set to −10 and the gap-extension penalty set to −0.5. These are standard setups for algorithms (e.g., BLAST) and many protein alignment tools. Scores were normalized by the maximum self-alignment score to account for sequence length differences. The off-diagonal scores among the four antigen systems were all close to zero or negative, ranging from −0.053 to 0.034, indicating very low global sequence similarity between these antigens.
The training, evaluation, and test datasets covered distinct antigen systems, ensuring no overlap between data splits.
This setup compels models to learn true binding determinants rather than memorizing antigen or antibody identities

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Significance testing rather than replicates. Each baseline is compared with MochiBind by a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs, with all p values below 0.0001 and the chi-squared statistics in Table S1. The paper reports no repeated training runs, seeds or confidence intervals on the accuracies. A sensitivity analysis is given instead: accuracy is stratified by the relative affinity gap within a pair, and it rises as the gap widens, with a large share of test pairs falling in the 0 to 10 per cent band that training excludes.

strengths.text: Per-antigen heterogeneity is reported instead of being averaged away: the affinity distributions differ markedly between antigens, and the authors show that retrieval precision depends on that composition.

quotes.text: The PEM and TRA datasets display bimodal distributions, likely reflecting clear distinctions between strong and weak binders, while VHH72 follows a right-skewed unimodal distribution, and PP489 exhibits an intermediate pattern. The number of strong binders and non-binders also varies across antigens: PP489 contains the highest proportion of very strong and strong binders, whereas TRA consists predominantly of weak or non-binding variants.
In the dataset of VHH72, a camelid single-chain antibody targeting the RBD of SARS-CoV1 with cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV2, the majority of the antibody mutations are good binders

limitations.text: Four antigens is a narrow base for a generalisation claim. Each rotation has two training antigens, one validation antigen and one test antigen, so a reported accuracy rests on a single held-out system and the authors themselves name dataset scarcity as the limiting factor.

diagram.title: Universal antibody-antigen affinity evaluation
steps: AlphaBind: four antigen systems with large antibody variant pools
stratified subsample, 10,000 variants each for PP489, PEM and VHH72 and 5,000 for TRA
sample 200,000 pairs per antigen, training pairs above a 10 per cent affinity gap
rotate antigens: two train, one validates, one is held out
model picks the stronger binder in each test pair
pairwise accuracy per held-out antigen, with a McNemar test against each baseline
TrueSkill global ranking, then retrieval accuracy and precision at K
diagram.caption: The pipeline as the STAR Methods and the results sections describe it.

quotes.text: To reduce computational cost while maintaining data diversity, we applied stratified sampling to select 5,000 antibodies per antigen following the same binding-affinity distribution as the full AlphaBind dataset. This sampling strategy follows the experimental design of the original AlphaBind study, in which PP489, PEM, and VHH72 are used for both finetuning and evaluation, while TRA is treated as a held-out antigen system for assessing cross-antigen generalization. As a result, for PP489, PEM, and VHH72, we sample 5,000 variants from the finetuning set and 5,000 from the evaluation set, yielding 10,000 antibody variants per antigen. In contrast, 5,000 variants are sampled from the TRA dataset.

Specifically, we sample 200,000 pairs per antigen for training, restricting selected pairs to those whose relative affinity difference exceeds 10%. This threshold ensures that the selected pairs reflect meaningful distinctions in binding strength, promoting efficient learning of robust and interpretable signals.
For the test datasets, no such thresholding is applied, allowing evaluation under realistic experimental conditions that include small and noisy affinity differences.

To rigorously assess the models’ performance on out-of-distribution systems, we employ a cross-antigen evaluation scheme. In each experimental configuration, two antigens are used for training (400,000 pairs), one for validation (200,000 pairs), and one for testing (200,000 pairs without threshold). For example, when the model is trained on PEM and PP489, the VHH72 dataset is used for validation to select the best-performing checkpoint, and the model is subsequently evaluated on TRA. This process is repeated so that each antigen serves as the held-out test set once.
to infer global rankings across all candidates, allowing the identification of top binders within each antigen pool.

gaps: The paper gives two different pool sizes for the AlphaBind antigen systems: the introduction and STAR Methods say approximately 30,000 variants per antigen, while the results section says each antigen is associated with 5,000 to 10,000 variants, which matches the subsamples the benchmark actually uses.
Retrieval accuracy and precision are reported only in figures, so no retrieval number could be recorded; only the Table 2 pairwise accuracies are printed.
Nothing is said about overlap between these antibodies and the pretraining data of ESM-2 or of the structure-based baselines.
The evaluation notebooks and the model code were not opened in this pass, only the README and the pair sampling script.

run_guide.summary: Get the published evaluation code at a pinned commit, install its environment, build the ESM embeddings and train or load MochiBind, then run the pairwise accuracy and retrieval notebooks.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 in a clean conda environment, with the repository's requirements.txt, or requirements-gpu.txt for GPU use.
A separate environment for the Graphinity baseline, built from requirements-graphinity.txt.
Precomputed ESM mean embeddings in a data_processed_esm_mean directory for full training.
Acceptance of the licence terms: the code is CC BY-NC 4.0 and the README describes it as a non-commercial research release for academic reproducibility. The AlphaBind data it ships are MIT licensed.

notes: Two numbers in the source disagree and a reviewer should know which this page uses. The introduction and the STAR Methods say each AlphaBind antigen system holds approximately 30,000 antibody variants, while the results section says each unique antigen is associated with 5,000 to 10,000 variants. The second figure matches what the benchmark uses: stratified subsamples of 10,000 variants for PP489, PEM and VHH72 and 5,000 for TRA. The structured size of 200,000 is neither of those: it is the number of sampled antibody pairs in the held-out test set for that antigen, which is the set Table 2's accuracy is computed on, and the test pairs carry no affinity-difference threshold. The published pair sampling script also requires both antibodies in a pair to have the same sequence length, a restriction the paper does not state. Retrieval accuracy and precision appear only in figures, so only the pairwise accuracies are available as numbers. The paper is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and the code repository CC BY-NC 4.0, so no source bytes are stored; the AlphaBind data the code ships are MIT, which the README states and links.
